newsitem.title: USA: U.S. budget negotiators say progress in talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. budget negotiators say progress in talks.

text.p: White House and congressional budget negotiators said Tuesday they made progress in the latest round of talks on a five-year plan to balance the federal budget.
But they added that some "very big issues" in disagreement needed to be decided by congressional leaders and White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles.
"This is an agreement that is going to cover about $9 trillion. I can safely say that 99 percent of that is not in dispute," Office of Management and Budget director Franklin Raines told reporters.

Enough major issues were left unresolved that the House Budget Committee put off until Thursday its public debate on the balanced budget plan. The Senate Budget Committee was now expected to hold its meeting on Thursday as well.
Raines and White House economic policy chief Gene Sperling held closed meetings with House and Senate Budget Committee leaders of both parties for several hours in the Capitol.

"We have reached many agreements and there are a few issues remaining and a lot of work to be done," Senate Budget Committee chairman Pete Domenici, Republican of New Mexico, said. "I think the remaining issues are not insurmountable. I look forward to resolving them tomorrow with our leadership," he added.
His Democratic counterpart, Sen. Frank Lautenberg of New Jersey, said the issues concerning the process of the budget debate were looming larger than issues of government funding.

He added that all sides were anxious to put the final touches on the plan. "Unless it's done it could pop open at any time. Because there are people on the edge who want to hang in for their last ditch stand against one program or for another. This is a fairly critical time."

On May 2 Republican leaders and President Clinton announced agreement on a five-year plan to balance the budget and cut taxes. Since then they have been working out disputes on what was contained in the agreement.
